name: Veinous Blood Red
lede: Veinous Blood Red is a dark, brown-black red from Werner's nomenclature of colors as Syme renamed it, named for the blood of the veins and set beside the brighter red of the arteries.

sections.title: A color named for a body fluid
sections.body:
Veinous Blood Red is number 96 in the chart of reds in Syme's edition of Werner's nomenclature, which Baty reproduces in *Nature's Palette*; Baty notes it is Syme's name for Werner's Blood Red [1][2]. The definition given is carmine red mixed with brownish black [1]. In the same run of reds it follows Cochineal Red and comes before Brownish Purple Red and Chocolate Red [1].

Each Werner color is tied to three examples, one from each kingdom of nature [1]. For this one the animal example is veinous blood, the vegetable one is the dark purple scabious (the "musk flower"), and the mineral one is the garnet called pyrope [1]. Earlier in the series sits Arterial Blood Red, so the list holds both blood colors, bright and dark [1].

Chocolate Red, two steps on, is defined as veinous blood red mixed with a little brownish red [1]. Baty illustrates the color with a watercolor of blood from a leukaemia case by Thomas Godart, made about 1852-61, and with scabious petals from a botanical plate of 1812 [1].

sections.title: The swatch
sections.body: The swatch is taken from an aged chart, and our library marks it as approximate [3]. It reads as a very dark, purplish brown, nearly black, which fits the recipe of carmine toned down with brownish black [1][3]. It is not the bright red many people picture for blood.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body:
In our archive of 23,781 paintings, this color covers at least five per cent of the canvas, within six units of color distance, in 987 paintings, or 4.2 per cent [4]. It is almost always a shadow color: 89 per cent of its appearances are in the darkest band of the picture [4]. These are photographs of aged, varnished paintings, so a match is not a pigment test [4].

The peak decade is the 1490s, in 20 of 215 paintings [4]. Painters who lean on it include Pontormo, in 5 of 13 works, about nine times the archive rate [4]. The strongest single match is Bartholomeus van der Helst's self-portrait of 1667, where it fills 92 per cent of the canvas [4]. Its company is [[aubergine]] and [[navy]], the other very dark colors that are not quite black [4].
